html:
Our Lady of Guadalupe is the Virgin Mary as Catholics believe she appeared to an Indigenous man, Juan Diego, on the hill of Tepeyac near Mexico City in December 1531. She became the central symbol of Mexican Catholicism and of Mexico itself.

The story, first written down in Nahuatl in the next century, says Mary spoke to Juan Diego in his own language and asked for a church on the hill. When the bishop wanted a sign, roses bloomed out of season, and when Juan Diego opened his cloak before the bishop, an image of the Virgin was printed on it. That cloth hangs today in the Basilica of Guadalupe, the most visited Catholic shrine in the world.

Tepeyac had been a sacred place before the conquest, linked to an Aztec mother goddess, Tonantzin. The Guadalupe image has a dark face and was soon called "La Morenita". This let Indigenous and mixed people see the faith as their own, a decade after the fall of Tenochtitlan and amid the friars' missions (see Twelve Apostles of Mexico).

The image grew into a national banner. In 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo raised it at the start of Mexico's war of independence (see independence wars), and rebels in the Mexican Revolution carried it too. Juan Diego was declared a saint in 2002. Each 12 December millions make the pilgrimage to Tepeyac.
sum: Our Lady of Guadalupe is the Virgin Mary as Catholics believe she appeared to an Indigenous man, Juan Diego, on the hill of Tepeyac near Mexico City in December 1531. She became the central symbol of Mexican Catholicism and of Mexico itself…
